result.summary: Æneas sails past Circe's coast and enters the Tiber, where Latinus, warned by oracles, welcomes the Trojans and offers his daughter Lavinia. Juno sends the Fury Allecto to madden Amata, Turnus and the countryside, war breaks out, and the poem closes with a catalogue of the Italian forces.

scenes.title: Past Circe to the Tiber
scenes.summary: Æneas buries Caieta, sails past Circe's shore with Neptune's help and reaches the Tiber's mouth.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk being transformed by Circe's magic if they land.

place.name: Coast of Circe's realm and Tiber mouth

scenes.title: Invocation and Latinus's House
scenes.summary: The poet invokes Erato and introduces old Latinus, his line, Lavinia and her suitor Turnus.
scenes.stakes: Latinus has no male heir and the succession is uncertain.

scenes.title: Portents and Faunus's Oracle
scenes.summary: Bees on the laurel and Lavinia's burning hair alarm Latinus, who consults Faunus and is told to await a foreign son-in-law.
scenes.stakes: Latinus must choose between his people's wishes and the oracle's command.

scenes.title: Eating the Tables
scenes.summary: The Trojans eat their cake-platters, Iulus jokes, and Æneas recognizes the fulfilled prophecy. Jove thunders approval and Æneas sends envoys.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans' long wandering and need of a promised home.

scenes.title: Embassy to Latinus
scenes.summary: Ilioneus pleads for a home; Latinus welcomes Æneas as destined son-in-law and sends gifts.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans need a welcome; Latinus risks defying Turnus and his people.

scenes.title: Juno Summons Allecto
scenes.summary: Juno sees the Trojans settled, rages, and sends Allecto to stir up war.
scenes.stakes: Juno fears defeat by fate and loss of her power.

place.name: Sky over Sicily and the underworld

scenes.title: Amata Driven Mad
scenes.summary: Allecto infects Amata with serpent venom; she protests, then raves as a Bacchante.

scenes.title: Allecto and Turnus
scenes.summary: Disguised as Calybe, Allecto urges Turnus to war; he scorns her, she reveals herself and inflames him.
scenes.stakes: Turnus risks losing his bride and falling under the Fury's madness.

scenes.title: The Stag and First Blood
scenes.summary: Allecto maddens Iulus's hounds; Ascanius wounds Silvia's tame stag, and fighting erupts with deaths of Almo and Galæsus. Juno dismisses Allecto.

scenes.title: War Declared
scenes.summary: Allecto retires to Amsanctus; Latinus yields, and Juno herself opens the gates of War. Italy arms.
scenes.stakes: Latinus loses control of his kingdom and Italy slides into war.

scenes.title: Catalogue of Italian Forces
scenes.summary: The poet lists the chiefs and peoples allied with Turnus, from Mezentius to Camilla.
scenes.stakes: Many of these leaders are doomed in the coming war.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses both names for Æneas's son.
Epithet of Diana; Hippolytus passage names her Dian and Trivia.
Another name for the Trojans, as are Dardans and Phrygians.

notable_quotes.reason: Iulus's joke fulfils the prophecy of the eaten tables and signals the end of wandering.
Juno's famous resolve: if heaven fails her, she will stir up hell.
Virgil signals the second half of the epic, a grander war theme.

analysis.text: Fate and divine opposition collide: destiny gives Æneas Latium, but Juno turns the peaceful welcome into war through Fury-driven madness.
The gates of War and the catalogue of Italian peoples link legendary origins to Rome's institutions, Augustus's Italy and the Claudian family.

legacy.text: Juno's line 'flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo' became famous and was used by Freud as the epigraph of The Interpretation of Dreams (1899).

fun_facts.text: The Temple of Janus in Rome had its doors open in war and closed in peace, and Augustus closed them in 29 BC.

language_notes.text: Hesperia means 'the western land', the Greek name for Italy. Here it names the Italian coast where Caieta was buried.
The 'shrill comb' and 'delicate warp' refer to a weaver's comb (a batten) pressing the weft threads tight on the loom.
'Mien' means appearance or bearing; Circe's drugs changed men from human form into animal shape, as Ulysses' crew were changed in the Odyssey.
Ausonian is a poetic name for Italian, from the Ausones, an early people of southern Italy.
Tyrrhenian means Etruscan, the people of central Italy, who later appear as allies in the war.
Saturn, an ancient Italian god, was said to have ruled Latium in a golden age; here he is the first ancestor of Latinus' line.
The 'branch cut off' is a metaphor for Latinus' son dying young, leaving no male heir.
The name Laurentines is explained by the laurel (Latin laurus); the tree gives the people and city their name.
Faunus is Latinus's father and an oracular rural god; his oracle sat by the sulphurous spring of Albunea.
Œnotrian means Italian, originally the name of a southern Italian people.
Old Laomedon's young chivalry means the Trojans; Laomedon was an early king of Troy.
Iulus jokes that they are eating their tables, the cake-platters; this unwittingly fulfils the prophecy of the Harpy Celaeno that hunger would make them eat their tables.
Phrygia's mighty mother is Cybele, the Great Mother worshipped on Mount Ida near Troy; Ida's Jove is Jove as worshipped there.
Pallas' tree is the olive, sacred to Pallas (Minerva) and a traditional sign of peaceful supplication.
"Missioned band" means the group of envoys Æneas sent; "Latium" is the region of Italy around Rome.
The fasces were bundles of rods carrying an axe, borne before Roman magistrates as signs of authority.
Picus, a Latin king, was turned into a woodpecker by Circe after he rejected her love. "Bridal jealousy" refers to her spurned passion.
"Quirinal staff" is the short, curved augur's staff (lituus); the "robe of scanty border" is the trabea, a short-striped ceremonial robe.
"Ausonian" is a poetic name for Italian; "Teucrians" and "sons of Dardanus" both mean Trojans.
The hurricane from Mycenæ is the Greek assault on Troy, led by Agamemnon, king of Mycenæ.
A poitrel is a horse's breast armour or breast-strap.
Circe was the daughter of the Sun; she bred these horses by stealth from her father's divine stock, mixed with a mortal mare.
Argos was Juno's favoured city; Inachus was its legendary first king or river-god. Pachynus is the southeast cape of Sicily.
"Destinies of Phrygia" means the fate decreed for the Trojans (Phrygians), which blocks Juno's own will.
Syrtes (treacherous sandbanks off Africa), Scylla (a sea monster) and Charybdis (a whirlpool) were the notorious sea-dangers Æneas passed.
Juno cites myths of punishment: the Lapithans were destroyed after the centaur battle, and Diana sent the Calydonian boar to ravage Calydon after being slighted.
"Fiends of the deep" refers to the powers of the underworld, whom she will call on since the gods above will not help.
Hecuba, Priam's wife, dreamed she bore a firebrand before bearing Paris, whose abduction of Helen caused Troy's fall. Here Lavinia is the new Helen.
"On this wise" is archaic for "in this way."
"Gorgon venom" refers to the snakes of the Gorgon Medusa's hair; Allecto, a Fury, has serpents in her own hair.
The Phrygian shepherd is Paris, who abducted Helen, wife of Menelaus of Lacedæmon (Sparta), causing the Trojan War. Amata likens Aeneas to him.
Inachus was the first king of Argos and Acrisius a later Argive king; Amata claims Turnus has Greek ancestry, so he is not wholly foreign.
"Hymen" is the god of marriage; his torch was carried in wedding processions.
"Evoe" is the ritual cry of Bacchus's worshippers (Bacchantes) in their ecstatic rites.
"Orgie" means the secret frenzied rites of Bacchus, not merely a revel in the modern sense.
Danae, mother of Perseus, was in legend cast adrift by her father and said to have reached Italy, where she founded Ardea.
"Her star is set" means Ardea's prosperity has declined; only its famous name remains.
A fillet is a headband; woollen fillets marked priestesses. The olive spray adds to her sacred disguise.
Ironic command: "spread the shield of peace" over Latium means to protect it by fighting. Allecto mocks Turnus to provoke him.
"Saturn's almighty daughter" is Juno, daughter of Saturn.
"Phrygian" here means the Trojans, from Phrygia in Asia Minor; Dardania and Teucrians also refer to them.
The Dread Sisters are the Furies, goddesses of vengeance; Allecto is one of them.
"The snare and the course" means hunting by trapping and by chasing with hounds.
The maiden of Cocytus is Allecto, a Fury; Cocytus was a river of the Underworld, so she is called its maiden.
"The reed" is the arrow, named for its shaft, which was made of reed.
"Clarion" is a shrill trumpet; here Allecto blows a herdsman's horn. "Tartarean" means from Tartarus, the infernal region.
"Brass" here means bronze weapons, which flash in the sunlight.
Ausonian means Italian; Ausonia was an old name for part of Italy.
Hesperia is "the western land", a poetic name for Italy.
"Sew" is an old spelling of "sow", meaning to spread rumours.
Acheron is a river of the Underworld; the gulf of Amsanctus was believed to be an entrance to Hades, which is why the Fury dives there.
"Saturn's royal daughter" is Juno, whom Virgil often names by her father Saturn.
"Teucrians" are the Trojans, named from their ancestor Teucer; "Phrygian" likewise points to Troy's region in Asia Minor, used here as a slur.
"Strain the throat of Mars to hoarseness" means they shout war-cries until hoarse, the war-god being imagined as the one cried to.
Virgil jumps to Rome's later wars: Getæ, Hyrcanians, Arabs, India and Parthia were distant peoples Rome fought or hoped to conquer.
The gates of War belonged to the temple of Janus at Rome, kept shut in peace and opened when war was declared.
The "Gabine cincture" was a way of girding the toga, with one fold tied round the waist, worn for ritual occasions; Quirinus is the deified Romulus.
Farm tools and fathers' swords are being remade as weapons, echoing the idea of turning ploughshares into arms.
Helicon is the Muses' mountain in Boeotia; invoking the Muses to 'ope' it asks for poetic inspiration before the long catalogue.
Aleides is Hercules, descendant of Alceus. He drove Geryon's cattle from Iberia (Spain) across Italy, and Aventinus is his son by the priestess Rhea.
Cæculus was said to be Vulcan's son, found among sparks or embers on a hearth, hence 'mid embers found'.
Clausus is the legendary ancestor of the Claudian family; the Sabines later joined Rome, as the line about shared homes recalls.
'Brand' means sword; 'primer's hook' likely means a pruning-hook, so the swords are curved sickle-like blades.
Hippolytus, killed by his own horses after his stepmother's false charge, was revived by Æsculapius (Pæon); Jove killed the healer for it. Virbius is the reborn Hippolytus.
The shield shows Io, turned into a heifer, guarded by Argus, with her father the river-god Inachus pouring his stream.

context_notes.text: Caieta was Æneas' nurse, who died on the voyage; the Italian town and harbour Gaeta is traditionally named after her.
Circe, daughter of the Sun, was an enchantress who turned visitors into beasts. Her island was identified with the Italian coast near Mount Circeo.
Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry; Virgil calls on her here at the start of the Iliad-like second half of the poem.
Turnus is king of the Rutulians and the favoured suitor of Lavinia, and he will be Æneas' chief opponent in Italy.
Lavinia is Latinus's daughter and the destined bride of Æneas; her burning hair is read as an omen of fame for her and war for the nation.
Latinus sleeps on the fleeces of sacrificed sheep, a rite of incubation, to receive a divine answer in dreams.
The Numicius was a small stream near Lavinium; the Tiber is the great river of Latium, later flowing by Rome.
Saturn and Janus were ancient Italian gods or kings of a golden age; Sabinus was the legendary vine-planting ancestor of the Sabines.
The Trojan royal line descended from Dardanus, son of Jove, so Ilioneus claims divine descent for Æneas.
Apollo's oracle sent the Trojans toward Italy, the original home of Dardanus.
Latinus recalls the oracle of his father Faunus, which said his daughter Lavinia must marry a foreigner.
Juno (Greek Hera) is Jove's wife and the Trojans' persistent enemy throughout the poem.
Bellona was the Roman goddess of war. The Rutulians were Turnus's people, Lavinia's rival suitors.
Allecto is one of the three Furies, goddesses of vengeance, who live in the underworld.
Pluto rules the underworld; Tartarus is its deepest region of punishment.
Allecto is one of the three Furies, sent by Juno to stir up war in Latium so the Trojans cannot settle peacefully.
Latinus, king of the Laurentines, had been told by an oracle of his father Faunus to marry Lavinia to a foreign husband.
Fawn-skins and vine-branch spears (thyrsi) were the usual dress and equipment of Bacchic worshippers.
Allecto is a Fury sent by Juno to stir up war between the Trojans and Italians. Turnus, king of the Rutulians, was Lavinia's suitor.
King Latinus had promised his daughter Lavinia to Turnus but, guided by oracles, now plans to give her to Aeneas.
The hurled torch is Allecto's means of infecting Turnus with madness, as she had earlier done to Queen Amata.
Tyrrheus is the king's chief herdsman. His family's tame stag becomes the spark of the war.
Trivia is Diana. Her lake, the Nar river and the Veline springs are all places in central Italy.
Saturn's daughter is Juno. The great Father is Jove, who would disapprove of the Fury's open interference.
Almo and Galæsus were killed in the skirmish that Allecto provoked over Silvia's tame stag; Galæsus was a peaceful man caught between the sides.
Latinus, king of Latium, is pressed to war by Amata, Turnus and Juno's agent, against the oracle telling him to give his daughter to a foreigner.
The cities named are real Italian towns near Rome, listed to show all Latium mobilizing.
Virgil begins this catalogue of Italian allies with a Muse invocation, imitating Homer's catalogue of ships in the Iliad.
Mezentius, king of Agylla (Caere) in Etruria, was an exiled tyrant who scorned the gods; his son Lausus is loyal and noble.
Messapus is a son of Neptune, the ocean god, which explains his invulnerability to iron and fire.
Camilla, a Volscian warrior maiden raised in the wilds and devoted to Diana, ends the catalogue as a striking final figure.

literary_notes.text: The Moon is given a human attitude, not scorning to light the way, as if she favours the Trojans.
Dawn's red sea, saffron robe and rosy car paint a vivid picture and mark the transition from night to calm morning.
The poet turns directly to the Muse, asking her for help, a traditional epic invocation.
Calling the new subject 'grander' signals that the war in Italy will be a greater theme than the wanderings.
Lavinia's blazing hair and smoke prefigure the fiery war that her marriage will bring to Latium.
Faunus's oracle looks ahead to Rome's world empire, linking the Trojan-Italian union to Roman destiny.
A boy's casual joke turns out to be the fulfilment of a fateful prophecy, so the weighty moment arrives lightly.
Hunger is called the end of death, turning the Trojans' wanderings into a kind of dying that now finishes.
Vivid, busy details of racing, archery and boxing show a lively, martial Latium full of young strength.
The palace is clothed in awe and terror, giving the old building a sacred, almost living presence.
The Trojan War becomes a hurricane that sweeps across Ida and makes two continents crash together.
Latinus's silent, fixed gaze shows a thoughtful, pious king who weighs omens more than gifts.
The ending on peace and the gifts of horses hints at the alliance, though Juno's hostility will soon disrupt it.
Juno's string of questions voices her disbelief and anger that all the Trojans' sufferings have failed to destroy them.
Juno sarcastically pretends her power and hatred are exhausted, while showing both are still fierce.
Comparing Lavinia's marriage to Hecuba's firebrand dream foreshadows another war caused by a bride.
Vipers that "burgeon" from Allecto's head compare snakes to plant growth, making her horror seem organic.
The snake merges with Amata's gold necklace and fillet, picturing how the poison turns her ornaments and her whole self into serpentine madness.
The poison is already working, yet she speaks with a mother's gentle complaint, which makes the coming outburst more disturbing.
Amata's frenzy is compared to a boys' top whipped in circles; the onlookers' wonder underlines how she is driven by an outside force.
Bacchus's goad is held in Allecto's hand, showing the god's rite perverted into an instrument of the Fury.
Turnus unwittingly dismisses a real divine message as an old woman's senile fancy, shown to be wrong a moment later.
Hissing snakes and stony eyes make the Fury's terror vivid and physical.
Allecto throws Turnus's insulting words back at him, turning his scorn into her threat.
Boiling water in a cauldron pictures Turnus's rising rage until it overflows into action.
Silvia's tender care of the stag shows her affection, which makes the stag's wounding more painful.
The wounded stag cries like a human suppliant, arousing pity and making the hunt's wrong plain.
A "dark harvest" of swords turns the battle into a crop of death, and the waves simile then shows the fighting growing.
Juno sarcastically calls the bloodshed the "alliance" and "nuptial rites" of Aeneas and Latinus, mocking the planned marriage.
Latinus is compared to a rock unmoved by waves, picturing his steadiness against the raging crowd, though he soon gives way.
Life is a voyage and death a safe harbour; Latinus laments only losing a peaceful end.
Juno strikes the gates herself, showing her contempt for Roman ritual and her personal drive to cause this war.
Plough and sickle swallowed up in the forge image the transformation of peaceful labour into war.
The poet directly addresses the Muses, asking for their divine memory to recall what mortals have forgotten.
The marching soldiers singing of their king are compared to swans in flight, making the army sound beautiful rather than fierce.
Halæsus is defined by hatred of Troy and loyalty to Agamemnon, giving him a clear motive.
Umbro's skill in healing serpent bites cannot save him from a Trojan spear, and the lake's mourning underlines the pathos.
Turnus's helmet crest of the fire-breathing Chimæra, raging more as blood flows, symbolizes his fury and doomed violence.
Camilla's speed is exaggerated: she could run over standing wheat or sea waves without disturbing them.
